steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on MAIDR, a system that makes statistical visualizations accessible to blind users by combining braille, text and sound. It should explain the accessibility problem, review prior work and its limits, introduce our approach, and summarize the user study.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Data visualization assumes visual ability; evidence of the accessibility gap
- Prior work on accessible and non-visual data representations
- Two limitations of current multimodal work
- Our approach: refreshable braille displays (RBDs)
- The MAIDR system and the plots it supports
- User study, research questions and findings

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Visualization assumes sight
  - adage "a picture is worth a thousand words": cognitive efficiency of good visuals
  - growing data -> visualization matters in finance, healthcare, politics, education
  - tacit assumption: visual ability -> paradox; convenient for sighted, impediment for blind
  - COVID-19 accessibility audit: only 14% of top Google search result visualizations highly accessible to screen reader users; much higher pass rates for "Born Accessible" sites (cite)
  - Joyner et al. (cite): over half of samples did not tell screen reader users a chart / chart type existed, data inaccessible
  - 144 sighted practitioners: ~38% say typically not accessible / not very accessible; 23% don't know
- Prior work
  - HCI, accessibility, visualization communities active in recent years
  - conceptual frameworks (cite); testable heuristics and audit guidelines (cite)
  - converting visual info into non-visual representations (cite): sonification (cite), natural language descriptions (cite), tactile graphs (cite)
- Limitations
  - recent focus on multiple representations complementing each other (cite)
  - (1) interactive multimodal work mostly basic plots: bar plots, time series line plots (cite)
    - also true for single-modality / static studies
    - Kim et al. review (cite): 56 papers, 1999-2020, ~80% limited to bar, line, pie, point-only scatter
  - (2) web-based multimodal still relies on sonification + speech-based text descriptions
    - constrained by current assistive technologies
    - verbal info (alt text, NL descriptions, lists, tables) go-to for decades via screen reader TTS (cite)
    - sonification (non-verbal, sound effects) growing interest to complement speech-only (cite)
- Our approach
  - represent visualization patterns and shapes on refreshable braille displays (RBDs)
  - fits blind users' existing computer access workflows, part of multimodal representation
  - prior: static 3d-printed / embossed tactile overlays on touchscreens -> audio-tactile graphics (cite)
  - no study yet on refreshable, interactive, automatic tactile methods with computer access tech for statistical visualizations
- MAIDR
  - inspired by everyday challenges of a blind data science educator; mixed-ability team co-designed / co-developed
  - Multimodal Access and Interactive Data Representation; auditory + tactile, verbal + non-verbal
  - four modes: Braille, Text, Sonification, Review (BTS+R); holistic framework for a spectrum of visual abilities
  - four plot types: bar plots, heat maps, box plots, smooth-line-layered scatter plots
- Study
  - 11 blind participants
  - RQ1: strategies to combine BTS+R within and across four visualizations
  - RQ2: to what extent RBDs fit existing computer access workflows
  - four question types: lookup, compositional, visual, non-visual (cite)
  - results: accurate interpretation; range of strategies shaped by past experience
  - takeaway: overlooked potential of refreshable tactile + other modalities; user autonomy

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
People say “a picture is worth a thousand words”, and this reflects how well-designed visual information is cognitively efficient. Society is producing more and more data, so data visualization is becoming more important in many sectors, like finance, healthcare, politics and education. But data visualization assumes something without saying it: that people can see. This makes a paradox, because what is convenient for sighted people can become an obstacle for blind people. A recent accessibility audit of COVID-19 data visualizations found that only 14% of the visualizations in top Google search results were highly accessible to screen reader users, and the pass rates were much higher for “Born Accessible” websites that were designed with accessibility in mind. Recent studies by Joyner et al. also show the accessibility challenges in data visualization. In over half of the data visualization samples they collected from different sectors, screen reader users were not told that a chart existed or what type of chart it was, and the underlying data was not accessible. Also, among 144 sighted visualization practitioners, around 38% said their visualizations are typically not accessible or not very accessible, and 23% said they do not know how accessible their visualizations are.

To address this gap, the HCI, accessibility, and visualization communities have been actively working on this in recent years. This includes conceptual frameworks for accessible data visualization, testable heuristics and audit guidelines for inclusive data visualization, and different methods that turn visual information into alternative, non-visual representations. These are things like non-speech sounds (sonification), natural language text descriptions, and tactile graphs.

Recent work has especially looked at using multiple representations together so that their strengths and weaknesses complement each other. These cross and mixed modalities give better non-visual accessibility, but there are two limited trends that we want to expand on. The first is that recent work on interactive multimodal data visualizations mostly only covers basic plot types like bar plots and time series line plots. This is still true when we look at studies that focus on a single modality or on static visualizations. A recent literature review by Kim et al. found that out of 56 papers published between 1999 and 2020 on vision-related accessibility in data visualization, around 80% only looked at four basic plots, which are bar plots, line plots, pie charts, and point-only scatter plots. The second is that web-based multimodal representation still relies on two conventional methods, sonification and speech-based textual descriptions. The main reason is that web-based visualizations and their multimodal interaction techniques are limited by what current assistive technologies can do. For example, verbal information like simple alt texts, natural language descriptions, lists, and tables have been the go-to strategies for accessible non-visual data representation for the past decades, helped by the text-to-speech technology of screen readers. On the other hand, sonification, which is non-verbal information using sound effects, has gotten more interest as a way to complement and overcome the conventional speech-only method.

- Our approach
  - represent visualization patterns and shapes on refreshable braille displays (RBDs); fits blind users' existing computer access workflows
  - prior: static 3d-printed / embossed tactile overlays on touchscreens -> audio-tactile graphics
  - no study yet on refreshable, interactive, automatic tactile methods for statistical visualizations
- MAIDR
  - inspired by a blind data science educator's everyday challenges; mixed-ability team co-designed / co-developed
  - Multimodal Access and Interactive Data Representation; auditory + tactile, verbal + non-verbal
  - four modes Braille, Text, Sonification, Review (BTS+R); holistic framework for a spectrum of visual abilities
  - four plots: bar plots, heat maps, box plots, smooth-line-layered scatter plots
- Study
  - 11 blind participants; RQ1 strategies to combine BTS+R; RQ2 how RBDs fit existing workflows
  - question types: lookup, compositional, visual, non-visual
  - results: accurate interpretation, range of strategies shaped by past experience
  - takeaway: refreshable tactile + other modalities overlooked; user autonomy

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
People say “a picture is worth a thousand words”, and this reflects how well-designed visual information is cognitively efficient. Society is producing more and more data, so data visualization is becoming more important in many sectors, like finance, healthcare, politics and education. But data visualization assumes something without saying it: that people can see. This makes a paradox, because what is convenient for sighted people can become an obstacle for blind people. A recent accessibility audit of COVID-19 data visualizations found that only 14% of the visualizations in top Google search results were highly accessible to screen reader users, and the pass rates were much higher for “Born Accessible” websites that were designed with accessibility in mind. Recent studies by Joyner et al. also show the accessibility challenges in data visualization. In over half of the data visualization samples they collected from different sectors, screen reader users were not told that a chart existed or what type of chart it was, and the underlying data was not accessible. Also, among 144 sighted visualization practitioners, around 38% said their visualizations are typically not accessible or not very accessible, and 23% said they do not know how accessible their visualizations are.

To address this gap, the HCI, accessibility, and visualization communities have been actively working on this in recent years. This includes conceptual frameworks for accessible data visualization, testable heuristics and audit guidelines for inclusive data visualization, and different methods that turn visual information into alternative, non-visual representations. These are things like non-speech sounds (sonification), natural language text descriptions, and tactile graphs.

Recent work has especially looked at using multiple representations together so that their strengths and weaknesses complement each other. These cross and mixed modalities give better non-visual accessibility, but there are two limited trends that we want to expand on. The first is that recent work on interactive multimodal data visualizations mostly only covers basic plot types like bar plots and time series line plots. This is still true when we look at studies that focus on a single modality or on static visualizations. A recent literature review by Kim et al. found that out of 56 papers published between 1999 and 2020 on vision-related accessibility in data visualization, around 80% only looked at four basic plots, which are bar plots, line plots, pie charts, and point-only scatter plots. The second is that web-based multimodal representation still relies on two conventional methods, sonification and speech-based textual descriptions. The main reason is that web-based visualizations and their multimodal interaction techniques are limited by what current assistive technologies can do. For example, verbal information like simple alt texts, natural language descriptions, lists, and tables have been the go-to strategies for accessible non-visual data representation for the past decades, helped by the text-to-speech technology of screen readers. On the other hand, sonification, which is non-verbal information using sound effects, has gotten more interest as a way to complement and overcome the conventional speech-only method.

To push the current effort of multimodal and accessible data visualization further, we introduce a new approach that represents data visualization patterns and shapes on refreshable braille displays (RBDs). RBDs can be integrated into the computer access workflows blind users already have, as part of multimodal data representation methods. Some researchers have pioneered static 3d-printed or embossed tactile graphics overlays on touchscreen devices to produce audio-tactile graphics. But no study has looked at refreshable, interactive, and automatic tactile representation methods using blind users' computer access technology for statistical visualizations.

Our mixed-ability team was informed and inspired by the everyday challenges that a blind data science educator had with different statistical visualizations at work. We co-designed and co-developed the Multimodal Access and Interactive Data Representation (MAIDR) system, which combines auditory and tactile representation, both verbal and non-verbal, with data visualization. MAIDR uses four modes, Braille, Text, Sonification, and Review (BTS+R), and it aims to give a holistic framework for interacting with data that works for a range of visual abilities. In this paper we introduce how MAIDR helps interaction with four types of statistical plots, which are bar plots, heat maps, box plots, and smooth-line-layered scatter plots, and each of them is tied to its own statistical concepts.

We did a user study with 11 blind participants. We wanted to answer two research questions. (RQ1) What strategies do blind users use to combine multiple modalities (BTS+R) when they explore data within and across four statistical visualizations? (RQ2) To what extent can RBDs be effectively incorporated into the existing computer access workflows for blind users when it comes to data visualizations? We asked the participants to answer four common types of data interpretation questions (lookup, compositional, visual, and non-visual) in the four statistical visualizations. Our qualitative and quantitative results show that MAIDR helped participants interpret statistical visualizations accurately, and participants used a range of strategies to combine multiple modalities, which were influenced by their past interactions and experiences with data visualizations. This work points out the overlooked potential of combining refreshable tactile representation with other modalities, and it raises the discussion about the importance of user autonomy when designing accessible data visualizations.

steps.text:

As society produces an ever-growing amount of data, the importance of data visualization grows in many sectors, from finance and healthcare to politics and education. A recent accessibility audit on COVID-19 data visualization revealed that only 14% of the visualizations in top Google search results were highly accessible to screen reader users, with significantly higher pass rates for “Born Accessible” websites designed with accessibility in mind [1]. Similarly, recent studies by Joyner et al. also highlight the current accessibility challenges in data visualization [2]. Over half of the data visualization samples collected from diverse sectors did not notify screen reader users of the existence of the chart or the chart type, and the underlying data was inaccessible. In addition, among 144 sighted visualization practitioners, around 38% said their visualizations are typically not accessible or not very accessible, and 23% said they do not know how accessible their visualizations are.

These include conceptual frameworks guiding accessible data visualization [3], testable heuristics and audit guidelines for inclusive data visualization [4], and various methods that convert visual information into alternative, non-visual representations [5], such as non-speech sounds (i.e., sonification) [6,7,8,9,10,11,12], natural language text descriptions [13,14,15,16], and tactile graphs [17,18].

In particular, recent work has focused on leveraging multiple representations to complement each other's strengths and weaknesses (e.g., [19,20,21]). While these cross and mixed modalities offer better non-visual accessibility, there are two limited trends that we want to expand upon. First, recent work on interactive multimodal data visualizations is mostly limited to basic plot types, such as bar plots and time series line plots [19,21]. This holds true even for studies focused on a single modality or on static visualizations. According to a recent literature review by Kim et al. [3], out of 56 papers published between 1999 and 2020 on vision-related accessibility in data visualization, around 80% were limited to four basic plots: bar plots, line plots, pie charts, and point-only scatter plots. Second, web-based multimodal representation still relies on two conventional methods—sonification and speech-based textual descriptions. This is largely because web-based visualizations and their multimodal interaction techniques are constrained by the capabilities of current assistive technologies. For example, verbal information, such as simple alt texts, natural language descriptions, lists, and tables, has long been the go-to strategy for accessible non-visual data representation over the past decades, facilitated by screen readers’ text-to-speech technology [14,16,13]. On the other hand, sonification—non-verbal information using sound effects—has gained growing interest as a way to complement and overcome the conventional speech-only method [22,6].

To push the boundaries of current efforts in multimodal and accessible data visualization, we introduce a novel approach that represents data visualization patterns and shapes on refreshable braille displays (RBDs), which can be seamlessly integrated into blind users’ existing computer access workflows as part of multimodal data representation methods. Although some researchers pioneered static 3d-printed or embossed tactile graphics overlaid on touchscreen devices to produce audio-tactile graphics [23,24], no study has yet addressed refreshable, interactive, and automatic tactile representation methods using blind users’ computer access technology for statistical visualizations.

Informed and inspired by the everyday challenges a blind data science educator experienced with various statistical visualizations at work, our mixed-ability team co-designed and co-developed the Multimodal Access and Interactive Data Representation (MAIDR) system, which combines auditory and tactile representation, verbally and non-verbally, with data visualization. Using four modes—Braille, Text, Sonification, and Review (BTS+R)—MAIDR aims to offer a holistic framework for data interaction that accommodates a spectrum of visual abilities. In this paper, we introduce how MAIDR supports interaction with four types of statistical plots—bar plots, heat maps, box plots, and smooth-line-layered scatter plots—each tied to its own unique statistical concepts.

We conducted a user study with 11 blind participants to answer two research questions: (RQ1) What strategies do blind users employ to combine multiple modalities (BTS+R) in their data exploration processes within and across four statistical visualizations? and (RQ2) To what extent can RBDs be effectively incorporated into blind users’ existing computer access workflows in the context of data visualizations? We asked our participants to answer four common types of data interpretation questions (i.e., lookup, compositional, visual, and non-visual) [25] in the four statistical visualizations. Our qualitative and quantitative results show that MAIDR facilitated accurate interpretation of statistical visualizations, and that participants exhibited a range of strategies for combining multiple modalities, influenced by their past interactions and experiences with data visualizations. This work highlights the overlooked potential of combining refreshable tactile representation with other modalities and raises the importance of user autonomy when designing accessible data visualizations.
